serbian-orthodox-church-downtown-pest.description: The Church of Saint George on Szerb utca is the Serbian Orthodox parish church of central Pest and, according to Wikipedia, the only Serbian Orthodox church in the capital today. Its Baroque building dates from 1733, its tower from 1752, and its garden wall holds old Serbian gravestones.
paragraphs: The Serbian Orthodox Church of Saint George stands at Szerb utca 4, less than a hundred metres from Váci utca in the inner city. Its full Hungarian name is Szent György nagyvértanú szerb ortodox templom, and it belongs to the Eparchy of Buda of the Serbian Orthodox Church. English Wikipedia describes it as the only Serbian Orthodox church in the Hungarian capital today, and it is a protected monument. The street takes its name from the community: Szerb utca means Serbian Street.

Serbian worship in Pest is older than the present building. A Serbian place of worship stood here during the Ottoman period, and some sources suggest a church on the site even before 1526. After Habsburg forces took the town, that church was destroyed in 1686. The authorities permitted a new one in 1695, which Patriarch Arsenije III Čarnojević renovated in 1698. The Baroque church seen today was built in 1733 to plans by András Mayerhoffer, an architect from Salzburg, and the bell tower followed in 1752. Archaeological research in 1959 confirmed that it stands on the site of an older church.

Inside, the church follows the traditional layout of an Orthodox church, and Hungarian Wikipedia notes a wooden railing between the women's area and the men's area, which sits one step lower. The iconostasis seen today dates from 1850. The original, by Stefan Tenecki, was damaged in the flood of 1838 and was replaced by a Neo-Renaissance iconostasis by a Greek artist.

The surroundings are part of the character of the place. A Baroque garden is enclosed by a stone wall, and the gravestones of Serbs who were buried in Pest are built into it. A Copf-style gate on Szerb utca dates from 1776, and at the corner of Szerb utca and Veres Pálné utca a ceramic image of Saint George slaying the dragon sits in a niche in the wall.

The church also records how small the community's footprint became. The larger Church of Saint Demetrius, damaged in the Second World War, was demolished in 1949, which left this church as the city's only Serbian place of worship. It is still in active use: in 2021 the parish celebrated its patron saint with a hierarchal liturgy led by Bishop Lukijan of Buda, a procession around the church along Szerb utca and a programme in the courtyard.
tips: This is a working Serbian Orthodox church. Check access and service times with the parish before visiting, and do not assume the interior or garden is open to visitors.
It is under a hundred metres from Váci utca, so it fits easily into a walk through the inner city.
From the street, look for the ceramic image of Saint George at the corner of Szerb utca and Veres Pálné utca and for the tower added in 1752.

queen-of-heavens-church-ujpest.description: The Queen of Heavens Church, or Egek Királynéja-templom, is the main Roman Catholic parish church of Újpest. Built between 1875 and 1881 to plans by József Kauser in a neo-Gothic style, it stands on Szent István tér, the main square of a town founded only in 1840.
paragraphs: The Queen of Heavens Church, in Hungarian Egek Királynéja-templom, stands at Szent István tér 13 on the main square of the former town of Újpest, today Budapest's 4th district. It is the district's main Roman Catholic parish church. Since 1993 the parish has belonged to the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest; before that it was part of the Diocese of Vác.

Újpest is a young town by Budapest standards. It was founded in 1840 on land given by Count István Károlyi, north of Pest. Its Catholics were first a filial of Dunakeszi and later attached to the parish of Fót, until Bishop Antal József Peitler of Vác made the congregation an independent parish in February 1870. A parish house and Catholic school were completed in 1873, and the parish was formally organised in 1875 with Vince Illek as its first pastor. He served until his death in 1905.

The church was built between 1875 and 1881 in the neo-Gothic style, to plans by the architect József Kauser, with Károly Bachmann as builder. Hungarian Wikipedia notes that two side aisles and a tower were added later to the original building. The tower is integral to the church and the aisles are joined to the main structure.

The bells carry some of the church's recorded history. There were originally five, and the middle bell, which weighed 310 kilograms, was lost in the Second World War; its place in the bell frame remains empty. Four bells hang in the tower today. The largest, named for King Saint Stephen, weighs 1,010 kilograms and was cast in 1924 by Ferenc Walser. The other three were cast in 1888 by Walser as well.

The square around the church tells the story of the town. It was called Templom tér, the Church Square, until it was named Szent István tér in 1928, and it became Újpest's main square after the town hall opened in 1900. A Reformed church built in 1878 stands on one side, and the town hall and the Újpest market are also on the square. Újpest became part of Budapest in 1950.
tips: This is an active parish church. Check access and service times with the parish rather than assuming the interior is open to visitors.
Szent István tér also holds the Reformed church of 1878, the town hall by Henrik Bőhm and Ármin Hegedűs, and the Újpest market, so the square is worth a short walk in itself.
Újpest lies outside the central districts, so plan the journey with the public transport journey planner before you set out.

holy-family-church-terezvaros.description: The neo-Gothic Holy Family Church at Szondi utca 67 was built in 1930 and 1931 for a fast-growing Terézváros. Heavily damaged on New Year's Day 1945, it was rebuilt and reconsecrated in 1948, and its high altar was later clad in marble paid for by the composer Zoltán Kodály.
paragraphs: The Holy Family Church, Szent Család-templom in Hungarian, stands at Szondi utca 67 in Terézváros, Budapest's 6th district. It is a Roman Catholic parish church in the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest. Unlike the older churches of central Pest, it is a twentieth-century building: Hungarian Wikipedia explains that Budapest's population grew sharply between the two world wars, which created the need for a new church here.

The architect was Gáspár Fábián. The foundation stone was laid on 28 September 1930 and the church was consecrated on 15 November 1931 by the auxiliary bishop István Breyer. In 1933 the parish became a vicarage, and its first vicar, Ferenc Sármány, was also the church's builder. Hungarian Wikipedia calls the style neo-Gothic. The Budapest library's description is more detailed: an eclectic design based on medieval church architecture, with Romanesque-style elements on the facade and English Gothic details, such as a large Tudor-arched window between the towers.

On 1 January 1945 the church was severely damaged. Sources differ on the cause, one speaking of a bomb and another of a chained explosive, but they agree that the furnishings were lost, including the altars, pulpit and confessionals, and that the organ was partly destroyed. Two things survived: the crucifix beside the pulpit and a statue of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux. Reconstruction began in September 1947, and Bishop Zoltán Meszlényi reconsecrated the church on 18 May 1948.

Later additions give the interior its present character. In 1955 the composer Zoltán Kodály, who visited the church often, paid for the marble cladding of the high altar and the pulpit. Péter Barba painted a secco in the sanctuary in 1961, and a statue of the Rosa Mystica was installed in 1985. A columbarium for urns was built in the basement and courtyard in 1996, the building was renovated in 2000, two new bells were consecrated in 2002, Zsolt Boromisza painted two new seccos in 2003, and the organ was rebuilt in 2006.
tips: This is a working parish church. Check access and service times with the parish before visiting.
The columbarium in the basement and courtyard is part of the site, so ask the parish which areas are open to visitors.
From the street, look for the large Tudor-arched window between the two towers, which the library description picks out as an English Gothic detail.

armenian-catholic-church-ujbuda.description: The Armenian Catholic church at Orlay utca 6 in Szentimreváros serves Budapest's Hungarian-Armenian Catholic community and is dedicated to Our Lady of Ransom and Saint Gregory the Illuminator. It grew out of a villa bought in the 1960s, and the parish centre was renovated with state support in 2022.
paragraphs: The Armenian Catholic church stands at Orlay utca 6 in Szentimreváros, in Budapest's 11th district, Újbuda. Its Hungarian name is Fogolykiváltó Boldogasszony és Világosító Szent Gergely-templom, and it is dedicated to Our Lady of Ransom and Saint Gregory the Illuminator. It follows the Armenian rite and belongs to the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest, according to GCatholic. Wikimedia Commons describes it as one wing of the parish building rather than a freestanding church.

A study published by the Budapest City Archives explains how the community came to be here. Most of the Armenians living in Budapest descend from the Hungarian-Armenian community of Transylvania. After the First World War and the Treaty of Trianon, many Hungarian Armenians moved to Hungary, and the community sought its own church and its own priest. For a very long time Roman Catholic churches in Budapest hosted the Armenian Catholic community.

The Orlay utca site came later. According to the same study, in the 1960s the Mechitarist priest Dániel Kádár gave up his family's properties and collected donations among Armenians in Hungary and Western Europe. With the money he bought a villa on Orlay utca, where a pastoral office, a chapel, a museum and a library were set up. The study quotes a community member who said that people went to the Orlay utca chapel as if to a second family.

In November 2022 the renovated Armenian parish centre was inaugurated. The National Catholic Register reported that Cardinal Péter Erdő and the Armenian Catholic Patriarch Raphaël Bedros XXI Minassian blessed it, that the Hungarian government funded the work through the Hungary Helps Program, and that the centre is to host educational and cultural projects and the archives of the Hungarian-Armenian community.
tips: This is a working Armenian Catholic parish, not a conventional sightseeing stop. Check access and service times with the parish before visiting.
Orlay utca is in Szentimreváros in the 11th district, so it fits a visit to that part of Újbuda.
The Budapest City Archives study shows a wrought-iron gate on Orlay utca, but do not assume the chapel or the parish centre is open to visitors.

pozsonyi-road-reformed-church.description: The Pozsonyi úti Reformed Church, known as the Hálaadás or Thanksgiving church, stands at Pozsonyi út 58 in Újlipótváros. Built between 1936 and 1940 to designs by Imre Tóth and Jenő Halászy, it has a classical portico, a separate tower and Bauhaus-influenced interiors, and its basement once sheltered people in hiding.
paragraphs: The Pozsonyi úti Reformed Church stands at Pozsonyi út 58 in Újlipótváros, in Budapest's 13th district, between Pozsonyi út, Garam utca, Gogol utca and the Újpesti rakpart. The parish describes the site as just north of Margaret Bridge, facing Margaret Island. It is a Reformed, or Calvinist, church, known as the Hálaadás temploma, the Church of Thanksgiving.

The congregation began in a first meeting house on Tutaj utca, consecrated in 1926, and outgrew it. The Reformed Church received the new plot from the municipality; it was marshy ground that had to be taken into account in the building. A design competition was announced in 1935. Imre Tóth won first place and Jenő Halászy second, and both took part in the construction. Work began on 6 December 1936 with a thanksgiving service on the empty plot, and the foundation stone was laid on 25 April 1937.

Sources describe the design in different words. WeLoveBudapest calls the church neoclassical, with Bauhaus features in the interior and the ancillary buildings, unusual aisle windows, a separate bell tower and Greek-style columns. The parish describes a classical building with a full-width portico, a central cross and a tall separate tower. Hungarian Wikipedia lists the style as Bauhaus. Construction took about four years, with stoppages caused by money shortages and the approaching war. Sulfurous water surfaced from the ground, which forced a redesign, and the tower was built on pile foundations. The church was consecrated on 8 December 1940.

The church was badly damaged in 1944, when it stood between German artillery fire from Buda and Soviet fire from Pest. The Danube-side entrance, part of the colonnade and the organ were hit, and damage marks remained visible until the building was restored in 1972. During the later war years the basement sheltered deserters, resistance members and mainly Jewish families, and pastor Albert Bereczky, who had led the construction, was recognised as Righteous Among the Nations.

Today the church is used for services, religious classes and Bible lessons, and WeLoveBudapest reports a basement theatre hall seating more than two hundred people. Hungarian Wikipedia says the crypt, with a stage and event hall, is rented out for various events.
tips: The parish website shows a liturgical calendar but no visiting hours, so check access and service times with the parish before going.
The church faces Margaret Island and stands just north of Margaret Bridge, which makes it easy to combine with a walk by the Danube.
The basement theatre hosts performances, so ask the parish whether anything is on during your visit.

rumbach-street-synagogue.description: Rumbach Street Synagogue, designed by Otto Wagner and consecrated in 1872, is an octagonal Moorish Revival synagogue in the Jewish Quarter of Erzsébetváros. After decades of decay it was restored and reopened in 2021, and sources describe it as serving as a synagogue, a museum and a concert hall.
paragraphs: Rumbach Street Synagogue stands at Rumbach Sebestyén utca 11–13 in Erzsébetváros, in the area of the former Pest ghetto. Hungarian Wikipedia gives it a second name, the Little Synagogue, to tell it apart from the Dohány Street Synagogue. It was built for the Status Quo Ante community, the more traditionalist congregation formed around the 1869 schism in Hungarian Jewry, and the Center for Jewish Art records Otto Wagner, then an emerging Viennese architect, as its designer.

Sources give slightly different dates for the start of construction: English Wikipedia says 1869, and Hungarian Wikipedia says 1 May 1870. The work was paid for by public donations. The prayer space was consecrated on 1 October 1872, and the use permit followed in May 1873. The building is of brick, in a neo-Moorish style, and the prayer hall has an octagonal plan.

The facade is symmetrical. Its two octagonal side sections are said to represent the biblical pillars Jachin and Boaz, and they are topped with lotus carvings and small domed towers that resemble minarets. The plaster is greyish-yellow with red brick stripes and blue enamelled bricks. Inside, an octagonal dome rests on eight slender iron columns with Alhambra-style capitals, and the walls carry gold, blue and red reliefs. English Wikipedia calls the design an homage to the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, though not an exact copy.

The building's later history was hard. In 1941 Jews were gathered in it before being deported to Kamianets-Podilskyi, and a plaque commemorates them. Worship ended in 1959, the roof over the Torah ark collapsed in 1979, the building was evacuated in 1980 and it was looted in 1982. After years of state ownership it passed to the Mazsihisz Jewish federation in 2005, and works began in 2017. The König-Wagner architects' office led the restoration, using Wagner's surviving plans and historic photographs, and the building was officially reopened on 10 June 2021.

The Center for Jewish Art records that in 2021 the building was open to the public and serving as a synagogue, museum and concert hall. Hungarian Wikipedia adds that it can still be used for ritual purposes and also hosts concerts, cultural events and conferences, and that a hydraulic mechanism in the middle of the octagon can raise or lower the Torah reading platform. Modern chairs have replaced the original wooden benches.
tips: Visiting arrangements depend on its mix of uses as a synagogue, museum and event venue, so check the current official information for opening times and tickets before you go.
It is also a synagogue, so ask the organisers what applies on the day of your visit.
Under the dome, look for the eight slender iron columns with their Alhambra-style capitals and the gold, blue and red reliefs.

kazinczy-street-orthodox-synagogue.description: The Kazinczy Street Synagogue is the great Orthodox synagogue of Pest's Jewish Quarter, built in 1912 and 1913 by the Löffler brothers in an Art Nouveau style influenced by Ödön Lechner. A Hebrew inscription crosses its brick facade, and the complex around it has included a school and a ritual bath.
paragraphs: The Kazinczy Street Synagogue stands in Erzsébetváros, in the heart of the old Jewish Quarter, and was built for the Orthodox Jewish community of Pest. In the late nineteenth century Pest's Jewish community had divided into three branches, the Neolog, the Status Quo Ante and the Orthodox. Sources give the street numbers as 29–31 or 27–29, so rely on the building itself, which dominates the narrow street.

The architects were the brothers Sándor and Béla Löffler. A competition was announced on 25 June 1909, and a jury favoured another design, but in May 1910 the congregation overruled it and chose the Löfflers' plans, which were approved in detail on 8 November 1910. The school and the community headquarters were completed in 1911 and handed over in 1912. Work on the synagogue began in the spring of 1912, and in July 1913 the architects submitted a plainer facade to cut costs. The use permit was issued on 29 September 1913.

The style is Art Nouveau, or Secession, shaped by Ödön Lechner's national style and by late Viennese Secession. The brick facade has a wrought-iron main gate flanked by two smaller entrances, coloured artificial stone decoration and a two-line Hebrew inscription from the Book of Genesis (chapter 28, verse 17). Inside, according to the sources, there are women's galleries, a central reading platform and a carved ark, with Transylvanian motifs in the wood carving, Zsolnay porcelain inlays on the columns of the eastern wall and windows by Miksa Róth. It can seat over a thousand people.

During 1944 and 1945 the building lay within the Budapest ghetto area. It was damaged in the Second World War and part of its furnishings were destroyed, and the complex was restored after 1945. By the end of the twentieth century the main synagogue had deteriorated and become unsafe to use. The congregation then used the ground floor of a neighbouring teacher-training college, now part of ELTE, and a small modern prayer house built in the building's west corner. The mikveh, or ritual bath, which operated here from 1928, reopened in 2004 after renovation.

Sources describe the synagogue today as the religious and cultural centre of Pest's Orthodox community. Hungarian Wikipedia says the main synagogue can be visited, but another source mentions renovation works and fundraising for repairs, so the position may have changed.
tips: This is an active Orthodox synagogue. Check access and visiting arrangements directly with the community and the official sources before you plan a visit.
One source gives the way here as metro line M2 to Astoria or M4 to Rákóczi tér, then a short walk to Kazinczy Street.
From the street, look for the Hebrew inscription along the top of the facade, a verse from the Book of Genesis (chapter 28, verse 17).

ujlaki-synagogue.description: The Frankel Leó Street Synagogue, known earlier as the Újlak Synagogue, is a neo-Gothic brick synagogue consecrated in 1888 and later enclosed by a 1920s residential building. It is the home of an active Neolog congregation in Buda's 2nd district, and it appeared in the 1999 film The Taste of Sunshine.
paragraphs: The synagogue at Frankel Leó út 49 is in Újlak, in Budapest's 2nd district on the Buda side. Its present name is the Frankel Leó Street Synagogue, and Újlak Synagogue is its former name. It belongs to the Buda Jewish Community, follows the Neolog movement and the Ashkenazi prayer rite, and has Tamás Verő as its rabbi. The community's website, frankel.hu, publishes its weekly prayer times and contact details.

The foundation stone was laid in 1887, the building was completed in 1888 and it was consecrated on 8 August 1888. Sándor Fellner designed it in the neo-Gothic style, on the site of an earlier synagogue that was about a hundred years old. It originally stood free of other buildings, with its entrance on what was then Zsigmond utca, now Frankel Leó út, among single-storey houses, a kosher butcher shop and community apartments. It measures about 21.5 metres by 19 metres and was built for about 400 worshippers.

In the 1920s a residential building was constructed around the synagogue. It was handed over on 1 August 1928 and was designed by Dezső Jakab and his son-in-law Aladár Sós, on the initiative of a former community president, Berthold Beer. The synagogue itself was rebuilt at the same time, given reinforced concrete floor slabs and joined to the residential building, so that today it sits inside the block.

Hungarian Wikipedia describes a three-bay facade of clinker brick with plaster detailing, stepped gables, pointed-arch windows and stone Tablets of the Law at the top. Inside are a wooden bimah, two seven-branched menorahs, an ark decorated with the Star of David and the Tablets of the Law, three women's galleries lit by pointed-arch windows and triple cross vaults. Marble plaques on the walls commemorate Holocaust victims and former chief rabbis.

At the end of the Second World War the synagogue was used as a stable, and the Jewish residents of the building were deported in 1944. A black marble plaque in the courtyard, unveiled in 2014, commemorates them. The residential building and the synagogue survived the siege of Budapest almost intact. The synagogue was used as a prayer house again under socialism and was completely renovated in 2000. It was also a filming location for Szabó István's 1999 film A napfény íze, The Taste of Sunshine.
tips: This is an active community synagogue inside a residential building. Use the contact details on frankel.hu to ask about access, and check prayer and service times there.
A memorial plaque for the residents deported in 1944 is in the courtyard, so ask the community before entering the building.
The synagogue is at Frankel Leó út 49 in Újlak, so it combines with a walk through that part of the 2nd district.
